clue.text: It helps to show car is in reverse, please

indicators.note: going in reverse means travelling backwards, so the little word before it is read from its end

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
to please someone is to delight them

explanation.surface: Instructions about signalling that a car is backing up, ending with a polite request.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs together as 'It helps to show car', a small lamp that makes a parked vehicle visible; 'please' is a verb, not politeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Small lamps at the front corners of a vehicle mark its width and presence to other road users at dusk.

clue.text: Opera setting in France

blocks.note: first meaning: the London theatre where Gilbert and Sullivan's operas were staged
second meaning: a region in south-east France, Savoie

explanation.surface: An opera whose action takes place in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The Savoy Theatre in London gave its name to the Gilbert and Sullivan 'Savoy operas'.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the London theatre built for comic operas and to an Alpine region now in France.

clue.text: Doctor with international organization, a man often tight

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
the United Nations
Ken is a man's name

explanation.surface: A GP with a global body, describing a colleague who is frequently stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' suggests mean with money; it is slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is often tight, slang for intoxicated, is habitually inebriated.

clue.text: A brother for Meg, Jo and Co?

definitions.text: A brother for Meg, Jo and Co?

blocks.clueFragment: A brother for Meg, Jo and Co?
blocks.note: surface reading: a sibling for the March sisters of Louisa May Alcott's novel
setter's reading: the sisters are Little Women, so their brother would be the male counterpart

explanation.walkthrough: Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy are Alcott's Little Women; Alcott's sequel is actually titled Little Men.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a male equivalent of the novel's title, and it also means an ordinary unimportant person.

clue.text: Dreary Frank does go haywire

indicators.note: a machine that goes haywire behaves erratically, so the letters come out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A dull man named Frank behaves wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go' looks like part of the indicator phrase but is also fodder; the indicator borrows it as well.
explanation.definitionFit: A godforsaken place is bleak, desolate and depressing, so the word describes dismal surroundings.

clue.text: Dog Latin quotation

blocks.note: first meaning: to follow closely
second meaning: a short familiar saying, often in Latin

explanation.surface: Mock Latin of the 'dog Latin' kind used for quotation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog Latin' is a phrase for bad Latin, which disguises the verb dog, meaning follow.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to follow them closely, and a well-worn Latin phrase quoted in speech is called this.

clue.text: A little bit of Murphy's firm

blocks.note: first meaning: a Murphy is slang for a potato, and a thin fried slice of one is this
second meaning: pleasingly firm and brittle, as fresh lettuce is

explanation.surface: A small share of a business called Murphy's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Murphy's firm' reads as a company name. A murphy is an old Irish-flavoured slang word for a potato, and in Britain the word means a packet snack (an American potato chip).
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a thin fried potato slice; the adjective describes food that is brittle, fresh and snaps cleanly.

clue.text: Links a lot of feet

blocks.note: first meaning: a series of connected rings
second meaning: a surveyor's measure of 66 feet

explanation.surface: A golf course covering a great many feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Links' suggests a golf course; a chain was also an old surveyor's measure, a hundred links long.
explanation.definitionFit: A series of joined metal rings is this, and so is an old unit of length used in land surveying.

clue.text: I am too old for love - that's laying it on thick

blocks.note: I am contracts to I'm
to be too old for something is to be past it
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone claiming to be beyond romance, and being accused of exaggerating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laying it on thick' sounds like exaggeration; it is literal, about paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the painting technique of applying pigment in heavy raised layers on the canvas.

clue.text: Adopts displaced small boy, for payment later

indicators.note: displaced means moved out of position, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: the letters rearranged
Ted is a short boy's name

explanation.surface: Someone takes in a refugee child, with costs to be paid down the line.
explanation.walkthrough: A post-dated cheque bears a future date, so it cannot be cashed until then.
explanation.definitionFit: A post-dated cheque carries a future date and is meant to be paid then rather than immediately.

clue.text: Boasted, see, 'aving supernatural inhabitants

indicators.note: the dropped aitch in this Cockney spelling tells the solver to drop the opening letter of the next word too

blocks.note: v is short for vide, Latin for see, used in references
a place with ghostly inhabitants is haunted, here said without its first letter

explanation.surface: A boastful Cockney claim that the house has ghosts living in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'aving shows the aitch dropped, and the same treatment strips the H from HAUNTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaunted is the past tense of vaunt, meaning to brag about or praise loudly, so it equals boasted.

clue.text: Weighty matter for a dolphin

blocks.note: a gram is a unit of weight
matter in the medical sense is the discharge from a wound

explanation.surface: Something of serious importance concerning a dolphin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weighty matter' looks like a single phrase for an important issue; it splits into a weight and the medical sense of matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Grampus is the name of Risso's dolphin, a grey toothed cetacean once also used for killer whales.

clue.text: Two oxen probably and fifty hind

blocks.note: a yoke is a pair of draught animals harnessed together, usually oxen
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A pair of oxen and fifty deer at the back of a farm scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Hind looks like the deer or the back legs; here it is the old word for a farm worker.
explanation.definitionFit: A hind was a farm labourer, and a yokel is an unsophisticated country person, so both mean a rustic.

clue.text: Ran in grandiose fashion

indicators.note: 'in ... fashion' asks for the letters in a new style, so they are rearranged
to fashion something is to shape it, so the letters are moulded into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sprinted in a showy, pompous manner.
explanation.definitionFit: To run an event or a business is to manage it, which is to have arranged and coordinated it.

clue.text: Collect a bee

blocks.note: first meaning: as a verb phrase, to gather together
second meaning: a bee is a social gathering, as a sewing bee

explanation.surface: Catch an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: A bee here is not the insect but a gathering for a shared task, like a spelling bee.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb phrase it means assemble; as a hyphenated noun it means an informal gathering of people.

clue.text: Mountain boy

blocks.note: first meaning: a Scottish mountain peak, as in the name Nevis
second meaning: a boy's name, short for Benjamin

explanation.surface: A lad who lives in the hills.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland the word is a common noun for a peak, and it is also a familiar male first name.

clue.text: Game -it's not worth much

blocks.note: first meaning: a table game of rolling balls into holes
second meaning: a trifle, something of little value

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on some pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: It names a pin-table ball game and also means a mere trifle or something unimportant.

clue.text: In both sets, I am disposed to lose my opportunity

definitions.note: the answer is the general phrase, without 'my'

indicators.note: things disposed are set out or arranged, so these letters are laid out in another order

blocks.note: taken as written, every letter rearranged

explanation.surface: A tennis player admitting a tendency to throw away chances in both sets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposed to' looks like 'inclined to'; here disposed is the anagram signal and 'to' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: To miss the boat is an idiom for failing to take a chance while it is available.

clue.text: Midshipman working with 20

definitions.note: 20 across is TOLERANCE, so the definition means having tolerance

blocks.note: Mr Midshipman Easy is the hero of Captain Marryat's naval novel
a machine that is working is going

explanation.surface: A junior naval officer on duty alongside another number.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the cross-reference: 'with 20' means with tolerance, tolerant.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone easy-going is relaxed and accepting, which is to say possessed of tolerance.

clue.text: They don't make fast relative speeds

blocks.note: a granny is a grandmother, a relative
knots are units of speed at sea

explanation.surface: Family members who are slow movers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' is not speed but secure: make fast is a sailor's term for tie up, which these badly tied reef knots fail to do.
explanation.definitionFit: A granny knot is a reef knot tied the wrong way, which slips and so fails to secure a line.

clue.text: Runner saving a city

indicators.note: saving here means except, so the named piece is left out

blocks.note: Atalanta was the swift huntress of Greek myth, beaten in a footrace
taken as written, the letter removed

explanation.surface: An athlete rescuing a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' reads as rescuing; it means except.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlanta is the state capital of Georgia in the United States.

clue.text: A way of paying for fish

blocks.note: first meaning: initials for cash on delivery
second meaning: a common white food fish

explanation.surface: How you settle the bill at the fishmonger's.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation stands for cash on delivery, a payment method, and the same letters name a North Atlantic food fish.

clue.text: Suitable, wanting nickel to harden

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the named element is missing

blocks.note: congenial means agreeable or suitable
Ni is the chemical symbol for nickel, removed

explanation.surface: Something fitting but short of a metal, needing to be made solid.
explanation.definitionFit: To congeal is to thicken or set from a liquid into a solid or jelly.

clue.text: The ability to endure and enact role that's complicated

indicators.note: something complicated is tangled up, so the letters before it come out muddled

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor needs stamina to perform a demanding part.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerance is the capacity to put up with hardship, pain or difficulty without giving way.

clue.text: Android - Bobby has to put up with him

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a word up means writing it from bottom to top

blocks.note: Bobby and Rob are both short for Robert
taken as written, then turned upward

explanation.surface: A policeman forced to tolerate a mechanical man.
explanation.walkthrough: Bobby suggests a British policeman; it is just a pet form of Robert. 'with him' rounds off the surface and gives nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: An android is a humanoid machine, a type of automaton built to resemble a person.

clue.text: One imprisoned in Greece; there's no hope for him

indicators.note: a prisoner is locked inside walls, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: GR is the international code for Greece
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man jailed in Greece is beyond help.
explanation.definitionFit: A goner is someone doomed or beyond rescue, so nothing can be hoped for in his case.

clue.text: Part of stair is erect

definitions.note: the answer is one who rises, a noun rather than a verb phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: the vertical board between two treads
second meaning: one who gets up, who stands upright

explanation.surface: A piece of a staircase stands upright.
explanation.definitionFit: The upright panel of each step carries this name, and so does a person who gets out of bed, as an early one.

clue.text: Weapon drawn by Munchhausen

blocks.note: first meaning: a tall English archery weapon
second meaning: to draw the ... is to tell tall stories, as the fictional Baron Munchhausen famously did

explanation.surface: An archer's weapon pulled by a famous baron.
explanation.walkthrough: Baron Munchhausen is the hero of comic tales of impossible feats; 'draw the long bow' is an old idiom for exaggerating.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a medieval archer's bow, and drawing it figuratively means exaggerating wildly, as the boastful Baron did.

clue.text: What all soldiers initially used to be

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each word in the phrase

blocks.note: the heads of the three words

explanation.surface: A wry remark on what every veteran once was.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of the verb to be describes a former state, which existed formerly but no longer.

clue.text: A character of “Great Expectations”, he has concealed a rise perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the word is only one possible arrangement of its letters
something concealed is hidden inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: he has contracts to he's
the letters rearranged, placed inside

explanation.surface: A literary quiz: one of Dickens's figures, a man, is hiding a promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's novel Estella and Miss Havisham are both heiresses; the definition is a type, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Several women in the Dickens novel stand to inherit fortunes, so the type of person fits one of its characters.

clue.text: Precise demand

blocks.note: first meaning: accurate in every detail
second meaning: to insist on and obtain, as payment

explanation.surface: A clearly stated requirement.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means strictly accurate; as a verb it means to require or extract something forcibly.

clue.text: He can't keep up - because he's holding a horse?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone falling behind the group
setter's reading: the word holds GG, a gee-gee or horse, in its middle

explanation.surface: A walker lagging because he is leading a horse along.
explanation.walkthrough: Gee-gee is a child's word for a horse, and the answer's middle letters are GG, so the word literally holds a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A straggler is someone who lags behind a moving group and cannot keep pace with it.
